record.paper_title: Some Open Problems Related to Creative Telescoping
record.original_question: Derive an order-degree curve for general D-finite functions, meaning a bound that describes how the degree of a telescoper can depend on a chosen operator order for telescopers of those functions.

evidence.quote: Problem 3.1 Derive an order-degree-curve for general D-finite functions.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero and let $f(x,y)$ be a D-finite function in two variables over $K$; that is, $f$ satisfies a system of linear differential (or, more generally, Ore-algebra) equations with polynomial coefficients whose solution space is finite-dimensional. A telescoper for $f$ with respect to $y$ is a nonzero linear operator $L = \sum_{i=0}^{r} a_i(x)\, \partial_x^{\,i}$, with $a_i(x)\in K[x]$ not all zero, such that there exists a "certificate" $g$ (D-finite in the same sense) with
$$L(x,\partial_x)\, f(x,y) \;=\; \Delta_y\, g(x,y),$$
where $\Delta_y$ is either the derivation $\partial_y$ or the shift $S_y - 1$, depending on the chosen Ore setting. Define the order of $L$ to be $r = \operatorname{ord}(L)$ and its degree to be $d = \deg(L) := \max_i \deg_x a_i$.

It is known empirically that, for fixed $f$, there is a trade-off: telescopers of higher order can have lower degree, and vice versa. For several restricted classes (e.g. bivariate hypergeometric terms, hyperexponential terms, rational functions), explicit "order–degree curves" have been established—functions $\Phi$ such that, for every integer $r$ in an appropriate range, there exists a telescoper $L$ for $f$ with $\operatorname{ord}(L) \le r$ and $\deg(L) \le \Phi(r)$, with $\Phi$ typically describing a hyperbola in the $(r,d)$-plane.

Problem. For a general D-finite bivariate function $f(x,y)$ (specified by an arbitrary system of linear Ore equations satisfied by $f$), derive an explicit order–degree curve: produce an effectively computable bound $\Phi$, depending only on the input data defining $f$ (orders and degrees of the defining operators, etc.), such that for every admissible order $r$ there exists a telescoper $L$ for $f$ of order at most $r$ and degree at most $\Phi(r)$.
artifact.status_search_result: Order–degree curves have been established for restricted classes such as bivariate hypergeometric terms, hyperexponential terms, and rational functions (Bostan–Chen–Chyzak–Li–Kauers and others). For general D-finite functions, order bounds for telescopers are known, but no explicit order–degree curve has been worked out as of recent reduction-based creative telescoping work (2024). The problem appears still open.

status_evidence.title: Order-Degree Curves for Hypergeometric Creative Telescoping
status_evidence.snippet: Order-degree curves are derived for the hypergeometric case, expressed as hyperbolas in the (r,d)-plane.
status_evidence.claim: Order-degree curves are established in the hypergeometric setting, not for general D-finite functions.

status_evidence.title: Reduction-based creative telescoping for definite summation of D-finite functions
status_evidence.snippet: Reduction-based creative telescoping extended to D-finite functions; focuses on order bounds.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work addresses telescopers for D-finite functions but does not provide a general order–degree curve.

status_evidence.title: Trading Order for Degree in Creative Telescoping
status_evidence.snippet: Bounds on degree of telescopers given as functions of the order for special classes.
status_evidence.claim: Trade-off between order and degree is known for special classes; the D-finite case is the natural open generalization.
